summary.text: Take \(n=18\): since \(\sigma(18)=39\) and \(\sigma(6)=12\), the successive denominator values are \(a(18)=6\) and \(a(6)=1=2^0\), so \(a(18)\) has the required property. But \(18\) does not, because that would require \(a(18)=6\) to be a power of two, whereas \(3\mid 6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\operatorname{denom}\!\left(\sum_{d\mid n}\frac1d\right)
\]
be A017666, where the denominator is taken after the fraction has been reduced to lowest terms. Equivalently, if \(\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\), then
\[
\sum_{d\mid n}\frac1d=\frac{\sigma(n)}n
\quad\text{and hence}\quad
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,\sigma(n))}.
\]
Indeed, the divisors are permuted by \(d\mapsto n/d\), so
\(
\sum_{d\mid n}1/d=(1/n)\sum_{d\mid n}n/d=\sigma(n)/n
\), and cancellation by \(\gcd(n,\sigma(n))\) gives the displayed denominator.

In the formulation of the conjecture under consideration, membership in A005153 is the condition that the A017666 value is a power of two. Thus, writing \(P(m)\) for “\(m\) belongs to A005153,” we have
\[
P(m)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists k\in\mathbb N\text{ such that }a(m)=2^k.
\]
The conjecture is therefore
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\qquad P(a(n))\Longrightarrow P(n).
\]
We disprove it with \(n=18\).

First compute \(a(18)\). The positive divisors of \(18\) are
\[
1,2,3,6,9,18,
\]
so
\[
\sigma(18)=1+2+3+6+9+18=39.
\]
Since \(\gcd(18,39)=3\),
\[
a(18)=\frac{18}{\gcd(18,39)}=\frac{18}{3}=6.
\]
Equivalently, the reciprocal-divisor sum itself is
\[
1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac16+\frac19+\frac1{18}
 =\frac{39}{18}=\frac{13}{6},
\]
whose reduced denominator is indeed \(6\).

We must now check the antecedent \(P(a(18))\). Since \(a(18)=6\), this is just \(P(6)\). The positive divisors of \(6\) are
\[
1,2,3,6,
\]
and therefore
\[
\sigma(6)=1+2+3+6=12.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(6)=\frac{6}{\gcd(6,12)}=\frac66=1.
\]
This also follows directly from
\[
1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac16=2,
\]
whose reduced denominator is \(1\). Since \(1=2^0\), the value \(a(6)\) is a power of two. Hence \(P(6)\) holds, and because \(a(18)=6\), we have established
\[
P(a(18)).
\]
Thus the antecedent of the conjectured implication is true at \(n=18\).

It remains to show that its conclusion is false there. If \(P(18)\) held, then by the definition of \(P\) there would be some \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
a(18)=2^k.
\]
But \(a(18)=6\), so this would say
\[
6=2^k.
\]
This is impossible. Indeed, \(3\mid 6\), so the equality would imply \(3\mid 2^k\). Since \(3\) is prime, Euclid's lemma applied repeatedly to the product of \(k\) copies of \(2\) says that a prime dividing \(2^k\) must divide \(2\). (For \(k=0\), \(2^k=1\), which is not divisible by \(3\), so that case is impossible as well.) We would therefore obtain \(3\mid2\), a contradiction. Hence \(6\) is not a power of two, and so \(P(18)\) is false.

We have therefore found a specific integer, namely \(18\), for which
\[
P(a(18))\quad\text{is true but}\quad P(18)\quad\text{is false}.
\]
Accordingly, the universal implication “if \(a(n)\) belongs to A005153, then \(n\) belongs to A005153” is false.
